patient.chief_complaint: Progressive confusion and personality change over 1 week in HCC patient on sorafenib
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. T. is a 58-year-old man with alcoholic cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma receiving sorafenib, presenting with a 1-week history of progressive confusion, word-finding difficulty, and behavioral change. His wife described increasing irritability, repeated conversations, and inability to balance his finances — activities he normally handles. He denies hematemesis or melena. He reports worsening nausea and diarrhea over the prior 3 weeks that his oncologist attributed to sorafenib side effects (sorafenib commonly causes diarrhea and nausea). His sorafenib dose has not been adjusted despite the diarrhea, which has been 3-5 watery stools per day. He has low-grade fever 38.2°C on admission. The moderate-difficulty features in this case include: (1) sorafenib as potential direct neurotoxin (sorafenib-associated encephalopathy is rare but recognized), (2) sorafenib-induced diarrhea causing electrolyte disturbance as HE precipitant (hypokalemia), (3) concurrent low-grade fever requiring SBP exclusion, and (4) the need to distinguish HE from sorafenib-related CNS toxicity. The key diagnostic finding will be ammonia elevation with supporting EEG changes and SBP exclusion.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Hepatic encephalopathy, grade 2-3, alcoholic cirrhosis + HCC on sorafenib — precipitated by sorafenib-induced diarrhea causing hypokalemia (K 2.8), hypomagnesemia, and dehydration with AKI

differential.key_features: PRES presents with posterior white matter T2 changes on MRI — excluded; no hypertensive crisis; sorafenib PRES is rare; this HE is from indirect sorafenib-induced electrolyte disturbance
CT head and MRI brain both negative for intracranial mass — HCC brain mets excluded; HCC typically metastasizes to lung and bone first
Creatinine 1.5 (AKI on CKD2) — mild uremia may contribute but ammonia 86 + cirrhosis makes HE primary diagnosis; creatinine not severe enough for primary uremic encephalopathy
PMN 188 — below SBP threshold; culture negative; low-grade fever explained by HCC

optimal_actions.expected_finding: Ammonia 86, K 2.6, Mg 1.5 — sorafenib-induced diarrhea as precipitant

optimal_actions.action: CT head — exclude hemorrhage, intracranial HCC metastasis

optimal_actions.expected_finding: Theta-delta slowing with triphasic-like waves — grade 2-3 HE

optimal_actions.action: IV electrolyte repletion: KCl + MgSO4; IV fluids for AKI; sorafenib dose reduction
MRI brain to exclude PRES from sorafenib
optimal_actions.expected_finding: No PRES — sorafenib direct CNS toxicity excluded

critical_actions: Sorafenib-induced diarrhea is an HE precipitant via electrolyte disturbance — not from direct CNS toxicity; do not confuse the mechanism
MRI brain excludes PRES from sorafenib — PRES is a rare but real sorafenib toxicity that requires different management (hold sorafenib, treat hypertension)
CT head excludes HCC brain metastasis — important in HCC patients with confusion even on treatment
AFP rising on sorafenib may indicate treatment failure — oncology reassessment warranted concurrent with HE management
contraindicated_actions: Holding lactulose/rifaximin while investigating sorafenib toxicity — HE treatment should continue regardless of investigation
Stopping sorafenib without oncology consultation — abrupt cessation may accelerate HCC progression
key_reasoning_points: Sorafenib-related diarrhea causes electrolyte disturbances (hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia) that precipitate HE — the mechanism is indirect via metabolic derangement, not direct CNS toxicity
PRES from sorafenib is distinct from HE — PRES is associated with hypertensive crisis and shows posterior white matter T2 changes on MRI; differentiation is critical as management differs
AFP trend monitoring is important in HCC — rising AFP on systemic therapy suggests progression; should trigger imaging reassessment even while treating acute HE
Sorafenib dose modification guidelines: Grade 2 toxicities (diarrhea, hand-foot syndrome) may require dose reduction to 400 mg QD; Grade 3 requires dose hold

red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute confusion to paraneoplastic syndrome from HCC progression or HCC direct liver failure; focus entirely on oncological workup rather than HE
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Rising AFP is clinically significant for HCC monitoring but the confusion is from HE (ammonia 86, hypokalemia from sorafenib diarrhea) — paraneoplastic neurological syndrome from HCC is very rare; HE is the correct primary diagnosis

red_herrings.intended_effect: Diagnose as sepsis/SBP as the primary cause of confusion; aggressively treat with antibiotics before HE workup
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Fever in HCC patients on sorafenib can be from drug fever, HCC (tumor fever), or infection; SBP excluded by paracentesis PMN 188; no other infection source identified; HE remains primary diagnosis with sorafenib-induced electrolyte disturbance as precipitant
